assessment.Existence of an interference: There has been an interference with the applicant’s right to freedom of expression. The applicant, a lawyer, was disbarred by the Ganja Administrative-Economic Court’s decision of 22 February 2019 (see paragraph 21), which directly restricted his professional activities and ability to express himself in his capacity as a lawyer. Disbarment constitutes a clear interference with the right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference was lawful as it had a basis in domestic law. The disbarment decision explicitly relied on the Law on Advocates and Advocacy Activity of 28 December 1999 and the rules of conduct for lawyers (see paragraph 21). The disciplinary proceedings were initiated by the Azerbaijani Bar Association (ABA), the competent body under domestic law, following a complaint from the Prison Service (see paragraphs 17-20).
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued legitimate aims under Article 10(2) of the Convention. The domestic authorities sought to protect the reputation and rights of the prison staff, as the applicant’s statements were considered to have damaged their honour and breached their right to the presumption of innocence (see paragraph 18), and to prevent disorder, as his statements allegedly gave rise to unlawful gatherings (see paragraphs 16-17). These aims correspond to the ‘protection of the reputation or rights of others’ and the ‘prevention of disorder or crime’ as provided in Article 10(2).
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The interference cannot be deemed necessary in a democratic society. First, while there may be a pressing social need to protect the reputation of prison staff and prevent disorder, the applicant’s statements concerned allegations of torture, a matter of significant public interest that warrants strong protection under Article 10 (see paragraphs 12-14). Second, disbarment is not the least restrictive measure available; lesser sanctions could have addressed any legitimate concerns. Third, the domestic authorities did not provide relevant and sufficient reasons to justify such a severe restriction. The applicant, as a lawyer, was acting in his client’s defence with a reasonable basis for his statements, having observed injuries and heard his client’s account (see paragraph 12), and he promptly lodged official complaints with the authorities (see paragraph 15). The ECtHR has emphasized that disbarment requires compelling reasons (see no. 81024/12) and that lawyers must be able to speak out about serious human rights violations (see no. 29369/10). The speed of the proceedings (see paragraph 17) and the context of systematic targeting of human rights lawyers in Azerbaijan (see paragraphs 29-30) further undermine the necessity of the interference.
